title: Kettle Hours
author: Sienna
notes: Converted from content/ by game/tools/import-sienna.js. Edit the source in content/, not this file.
contentWarning: This game touches on stress, low mood, anxiety, grief, self-harm and suicide. Heavier scenes have a content note and can be skipped. You can pause, or open "Need help now?", at any time.

moodWeather.note: Mood is shown only through art and behaviour, never as a label to the player.

skills.name: Open Door
skills.description: Ask open questions that invite more than yes or no: 'How have things been?' rather than 'You OK?'

skills.name: Steady Voice
skills.description: Keep your own tone calm and slow when someone else is overwhelmed. Calm is catching.

skills.name: Echo Back
skills.description: Say back what you heard in your own words so the person knows you've understood.

skills.name: The Quiet Chair
skills.description: Let a silence sit. People often say the important thing after a pause.

skills.name: Sharp Eyes
skills.description: Notice changes from someone's usual self: habits, appearance, energy, mood.

skills.name: Ask Plainly
skills.description: If you're worried someone is thinking about suicide, ask them directly and calmly. Asking doesn't put the idea in their head.

skills.name: Stay Close
skills.description: In a crisis, stay with the person (or keep someone with them) while help is on its way.

skills.name: Call Now
skills.description: Know when to call 999, NHS 111 or Samaritans 116 123, and do it without delay.

skills.name: Know Your Limit
skills.description: You can be a good listener without being someone's therapist. Passing on to a professional is part of helping.

skills.name: Their Way
skills.description: Ask what the person wants and needs. Support works best when it's built around them.

skills.name: Kind but Honest
skills.description: Never promise to keep a secret that might put someone at risk, especially someone under 18. Tell them who you'll need to involve and why.

skills.name: Refill Your Cup
skills.description: Rest, eat and talk to someone yourself. You can't pour from an empty pot.

skills.name: Myth Buster
skills.description: Swap a stigmatising word or story for an accurate, respectful one.

skills.name: Signpost
skills.description: Know where to point people: GP, NHS 111, Samaritans, school staff, workplace support, local services.

skills.name: Small Changes
skills.description: Talk with a colleague about changes to how, when or where they work that would help them stay well.

skills.name: Plan Ahead
skills.description: Help someone write down what keeps them well, their early warning signs and what helps when things slip.

skills.name: The Long Game
skills.description: Recovery has ups and downs. Keep showing up after the crisis has passed.

guides.title: Body and mind
guides.body: Sleep, food, movement, pain and illness all affect how we feel, and feelings affect the body too: tight chest, churning stomach, headaches. Looking after one helps the other.

guides.title: What piles up
guides.body: Money worries, losing work, caring for someone, loneliness, discrimination, loss, and big changes can all push someone's mood down. It usually isn't one thing. It's how many things land at once, and how much support someone has.

guides.title: Low mood and depression
guides.body: Everyone has sad days. If someone feels low or empty most days for a couple of weeks or more, loses interest in things, sleeps or eats very differently, or feels hopeless, it's worth seeing a GP. Depression is common and treatable.

guides.title: Panic attacks
guides.body: A panic attack can feel like a heart attack: pounding heart, shaking, struggling to breathe, feeling doomed. Stay calm and stay with them. Help them breathe slowly and notice things around them. It usually peaks within minutes. Call 999 if there's chest pain, it's the first time with no clear cause, or they don't recover.

guides.title: Talking therapies
guides.body: In England, people aged 16 and over can refer themselves to NHS talking therapies for anxiety and depression, often without seeing a GP first. A GP can also help with options. Waiting times vary by area.

guides.title: Bipolar disorder
guides.body: Bipolar disorder involves periods of very low mood and periods of very high or 'speeded up' mood. Signs of a high can include needing little sleep, talking fast, racing ideas, big plans and overspending. Treatment, routine and knowing your early signs help many people live well.

guides.title: Psychosis
guides.body: Psychosis means losing some contact with reality: hearing or seeing things others don't, or holding beliefs that aren't shared, often frightening ones. Stay calm. Don't argue or play along. Focus on how they feel. Encourage contact with a GP or NHS 111, and call 999 if anyone is in danger. Getting help early makes a real difference.

guides.title: Recovering from psychosis
guides.body: Many people recover from psychosis and go back to work, study and the things they love. Specialist early intervention teams support people, often for several years. Routine, sleep, steady relationships and avoiding street drugs all help.

guides.title: If someone tells you they self-harm
guides.body: Stay calm and thank them for telling you. Don't panic, shame them or demand they stop. Check whether an injury needs medical care. Never promise to keep it secret if they're under 18 or at risk. Help them reach a trusted adult, a GP or Childline (0800 1111, under 19s).

guides.title: Eating difficulties
guides.body: Skipping meals, strict rules about food, or hiding eating can be signs that someone is struggling. Talk about feelings, not food, weight or looks. Encourage them to talk to a GP or a trusted adult.

guides.title: If someone may be suicidal
guides.body: Ask clearly: 'Are you thinking about suicide?' Asking does not put the idea in their head. Listen without judging. If they're in immediate danger, call 999 and stay with them. If not, help them contact a GP, NHS 111 or Samaritans (116 123) today. Don't keep it secret.

guides.title: Phobias
guides.body: A phobia is an intense fear of a situation or thing that's far bigger than the actual danger, such as lifts, needles or flying. People often plan their lives around avoiding it. Talking therapy, usually facing the fear in small, planned steps, works well for many people.

guides.title: Myth or fact?
guides.body: Mental health problems are common, aren't a sign of weakness, and people can and do recover. Words matter: 'a person with schizophrenia', not 'a schizophrenic'. Jokes and headlines that mock illness make it harder for people to ask for help.

guides.title: Danger and mental illness
guides.body: Most people with mental illness are never violent. People with severe mental illness are more likely to be harmed by others than to harm anyone. Headlines that suggest otherwise feed fear and stop people asking for help.

guides.title: Ripples
guides.body: Mental ill health affects families, friends and workplaces too. Partners may become carers and children may notice more than adults think. Carers deserve support of their own, and simple, honest explanations help children.

guides.title: Disability and adjustments
guides.body: Under the Equality Act 2010, a mental health condition can count as a disability if it has a substantial, long-term effect on everyday life. Employers must then consider reasonable adjustments, such as changes to hours, tasks or breaks. (Great Britain: England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has its own, similar laws.)

guides.title: Why employers should care
guides.body: Employers have legal duties to protect their staff's health, including mental health. That includes looking at work stress as a risk, as well as not discriminating. It also makes sense: supported staff stay longer, take less time off and do better work. (Great Britain: England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has its own, similar laws.)

guides.title: Coming back to work
guides.body: After time off, many people return gradually, with fewer hours or lighter duties at first, agreed with their employer and sometimes suggested on a fit note. Regular, private check-ins help adjust the plan.

guides.title: Wellbeing plans
guides.body: A wellbeing plan is written by the person themselves, with help if they want it. It covers what keeps them well, early warning signs, what makes things harder, what helps, and who to contact. Anyone can have one, with or without a diagnosis. Review it now and then.

guides.title: Setbacks
guides.body: Recovery is rarely a straight line. Anniversaries, stress or tiredness can bring bad days back. A setback doesn't wipe out the progress someone has made. Notice it, be kind about it, and use what's helped before.

guides.title: Where to get help
guides.body: GP: first stop for most worries. NHS 111: urgent advice. Samaritans 116 123: free, any time. Childline 0800 1111: under 19s. 999 or A&E: if someone's life is at risk. Free debt advice services can help with money worries. Friends, family and community groups matter too.

guides.title: Why people don't ask
guides.body: People often don't know where to go, feel ashamed, worry about their job, think help costs money, face language barriers or long waits, or believe they should cope alone. Each barrier you remove makes asking easier.

guides.title: Looking after the helper
guides.body: Supporting someone can be draining. You aren't responsible for fixing them. Know your limits, pass things on to professionals, take breaks, and talk to someone yourself, without breaking the other person's trust.

guides.title: Your energy
guides.body: Helpers run out too. Sleep, food, time off and people who listen to you aren't luxuries. They're how you keep going.

guides.title: What you did
guides.body: Noticing. Asking. Listening without judging. Knowing when it's urgent. Pointing to the right help. Staying with someone over time. You don't need to be an expert to do these things, and you should never try to diagnose anyone. That's a job for professionals.

rose.name: Auntie Rose
rose.blurb: Retired café owner, your mentor. Ran the café for thirty years. Calls in on Sundays, notices everything, and reminds you to eat.

maggie.name: Maggie Hollis
maggie.blurb: Regular, retired school librarian. Widowed last spring. Always orders a scone she rarely finishes. Sharp wit, softer than she lets on.

dev.name: Dev Okafor
dev.blurb: Regular, sixth-form student. Revises in the window seat with three highlighters and too much coffee. Wants to study engineering.

tom.blurb: Regular, self-employed builder. Loud laugh, big tips, fixes the café door for free. Lately quieter, and his van's been parked up.

priya.name: Priya Nair
priya.blurb: Regular, nurse on night shifts. Comes in at 8 a.m. after nights for toast and silence. Looks after everyone except herself.

kit.name: Kit Morgan
kit.blurb: Regular, Year 11 pupil, Maggie's former library helper. Draws comics on napkins. Funny, guarded, wears long sleeves even when it's warm.

sam.name: Sam Achterberg
sam.blurb: Your café assistant. Makes the best flat white on the street and remembers every regular's order. Has bipolar disorder, well managed.

jordan.name: Jordan Bell
jordan.blurb: Regular, delivery rider. Always in a hurry, always polite. Collects vinyl and talks about it to anyone who'll listen.

nell.blurb: Regular, editor of the Larkspur Ledger. Runs the local paper and knows everyone's business. Takes the stairs everywhere, never the lift.

chapters.title: Opening Up

steps.prompt: Make Auntie Rose something warm while you talk.
Make Sam Achterberg something warm while you talk.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Keys, float, and the temperamental grinder. That's the café. The rest of the job is people.

meta.summary: Rose hands over the keys and shows you that everyone's mood shifts like weather.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Look out of the window. Same street every day, different sky every day. Folk are like that. Nobody's all sunshine or all storm. We all move up and down, and most of the time we drift back.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Your job isn't to fix the weather. It's to notice it, and to be someone people can talk to when it turns.

options.text: How do I notice it without being nosy?
I'm here to sell coffee, Rose.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: You learn their usual. When the usual changes, that's your cue. Not to diagnose. Just to say hello properly.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: So was I, love. Thirty years of it. You'd be amazed how often the coffee was the excuse.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Morning, boss! Maggie's at table three, scone, Earl Grey. Dev's in the window seat: flat white, extra shot, which I'd question.
Maggie's scone sits untouched. Her cardigan is buttoned wrong. Last week, Sam says, she was doing the crossword in pen. Today the paper isn't open.

options.text: Wander over with a fresh pot and say hello.
Leave her be. She's probably just tired.
Call across: 'Cheer up, Maggie, it might never happen!'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Oh, you didn't have to. Rose always did this too. Spying, I called it.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: I'm fine. Just haven't been sleeping. The house is very quiet at night these days.

options.text: 'Quiet in what way?'
'Have you tried camomile? Works for me.'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Harold used to snore like a ferry horn. I'd give anything to be kept awake by it again.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: I've a cupboard full of camomile, dear. That's not really the problem.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Anyway. I'll finish my scone. Same time tomorrow?
Maggie leaves early, the scone wrapped in a napkin she forgets on the table.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: It already has, love. Last April.
She leaves her tea half drunk. Sam winces. Rose gives you a look that says: we'll talk later.
Small things, noticed early. That's the whole trick, Rose says on her way out.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Tomorrow's another chance. Same tables, same faces. Watch the usual.

bg.alt: Same Table, Different Maggie: cafe table three

bg.alt: Same Table, Different Maggie: cafe table three

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Changes on their own don't prove anything, love. But a few together, over weeks, are worth a gentle word.

options.text: 'I noticed you haven't done the crossword. Not like you. How are things?'
'You look a bit of a mess today, Maggie.'
'Maggie, I think you've got depression.'
Just say hello for now and keep an eye out.

bg.alt: Same Table, Different Maggie: cafe table three

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Thank you so much. Just what a widow wants to hear.

options.text: 'Sorry, that came out wrong. I just wondered how you are.'

bg.alt: Same Table, Different Maggie: cafe table three

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Do you now? And when did you qualify?

bg.alt: Same Table, Different Maggie: cafe table three

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: (quietly, later) Never put a name on it for them, love. Guess wrong and you can scare someone, or make them shut the door. Guess right and it's still not ours to say. Notice, ask, and point them to the GP.

options.text: 'Got it. Notice and ask. Leave the naming to the GP.'

bg.alt: Same Table, Different Maggie: cafe table three

steps.text: Noticing is where it starts. You don't need to know what's wrong, just that something might be.
It's 4 p.m. Dev has been here since nine. Four empty cups. His leg won't stop bouncing, and he's reading the same page over and over.

options.text: Bring him a glass of water and a cheese toastie, on the house.
Ask if he wants another coffee.

meta.summary: Dev is on his fourth coffee and hasn't eaten. A first proper conversation.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: I didn't order this. Oh. Thanks. I forgot about lunch, I think. And breakfast.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Yeah. Go on. Make it a large. Mocks start Monday and I know literally nothing.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Sorry, I'm fine. Just exams. Everyone's stressed.

options.text: 'Everyone is, but how is it for you?'
'You'll be fine, you're clever.'
'Honestly, mocks don't even count.'

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Bad, sort of? I lie in bed and my brain just lists everything I haven't revised. Then my heart goes really fast. I've been sleeping, like, four hours.

options.text: 'That sounds exhausting. Four hours and four coffees is a rough mix.'
'Just go to bed earlier.'

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Everyone says that. It doesn't feel like it at 3 a.m.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: They count to my mum. They count for predicted grades.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: I didn't think of it like that. The coffee makes me jittery, then I can't sleep, so I need more coffee.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Right. Yeah. Sure.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Can I... come back tomorrow? It's quieter here than home.

options.text: 'The window seat's yours. Maybe decaf after lunch?'
'Sure, just buy something.'

steps.text: Dev laughs, a real one. He eats the whole toastie.
Dev nods and packs up, still jittery.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: So. First week. Who's your weather report?

options.text: 'Maggie's grey. Dev's all storm clouds and caffeine.'
'Busy. Didn't really get a chance to notice.'

meta.summary: Rose and you review the week. Introduces your own energy.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: And you? You've not sat down since Tuesday. You had a biscuit for lunch. I counted.

options.text: 'I'm fine. Busy is good.'
'Honestly? Shattered.'

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Good. Saying it is the first bit. Proper lunch, a day off, and someone you can moan to. That's me, by the way.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: That's what I said for ten years. Then I had a winter where I couldn't get out of bed. Look after the person behind the counter too.
Your energy affects what you can offer. When it's low, fewer patient replies will appear. Rest restores it.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: (to yourself) Money worries and drinking can feed each other. Worth asking about, kindly, not as an accusation.

steps.text: Tom used to come in at 7 with his crew and order six bacon rolls. This week he's come in alone at 11, three days running. Black coffee. No roll.

meta.summary: Tom's work has dried up. Pressures stack, some short-lived, some lasting.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Don't look at me like that. Diet. Ha.

options.text: 'I've missed the bacon roll crew. How's work?'
'Diet suits you, mate!'

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Cheers.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Big job in Harbridge fell through. Developer went bust owing me eleven grand. I've had to let the lads go.

PLANNER: Tom's week fills up with tiles. Unpaid invoice. Van finance due. Letting the lads go. Partner Lena's hours cut at the care home. Daughter Poppy's school trip money. Some of these tiles will clear in a month. Others look set to stay.

options.text: Sort them: which might pass, which could last?
Skip the planner.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: And I'm sleeping on the sofa so I don't wake Lena when I'm up at 3 doing sums. Have a couple of cans to switch off. Well. A few.

options.text: 'That's a lot landing at once. The cans helping, or just quietening it for a bit?'
'Everyone has a drink, nothing wrong with that.'
'You need to stop drinking, Tom.'

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Quieter for an hour. Then worse. I'm snapping at Poppy. That's not me.

options.text: 'Have you talked to anyone about the money side? There's free debt advice.'
'Something will turn up.'

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Exactly. Bloke's allowed a drink.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Right. I'll take this to go.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Free? Didn't know that was a thing. Maybe. I'll think about it.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Yeah. Course it will.
Tom leaves the café door open, then comes back and fixes the sticky hinge he spotted. Old habits.
Tom heads off. The van stays parked outside his house all week.
Tom doesn't come in the next day.

steps.prompt: Make Dev Okafor something warm while you talk.

steps.text: The bell clatters. A tray drops. Dev is half out of the window seat, gripping the table. He's breathing fast and shallow, pale, staring at nothing.

meta.summary: Dev has a panic attack in the café. Calm, not crowding, and knowing when it would need medical help.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: I can't, I can't breathe, my heart, something's wrong, I think I'm dying.

options.text: Kneel beside him, speak low and slow: 'Dev, it's me. I'm here. You're safe in the café.'
Shout to Sam: 'Call an ambulance!'
'Calm down! Just calm down!'

steps.text: Being told to calm down makes it worse. Dev's breathing speeds up. Sam steps in quietly and moves the onlookers away.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Hang on, boss. Is he hurt? Has he got chest pain or a condition we know about? Let's check first. If we're not sure, we ring 999 and ask.
You ask Dev simple questions. No history of heart problems. He's had 'funny turns' before at night, when he's worried about exams. He nods when you ask if this feels like those.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: Your choice: what helps now?

options.text: Breathe slowly with him, counting out loud, and let him set the pace.
Get him to breathe into a paper bag.
Gather a crowd to give him air and reassurance.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Not the bag. It's an old idea and can be unsafe. Just slow breathing with him.
More faces make it harder. You ask people to give him some space and turn the music down.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: In... two, three, four. And out... slowly. You're doing it. Feel your feet on the floor. Tell me three things you can see.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: The... the cake stand. Sam's ugly jumper. The rain. Okay. Okay. It's going.
After about ten minutes Dev's breathing is back to normal. He's exhausted and embarrassed.

options.text: 'Nothing to be embarrassed about. That sounded like a panic attack. Horrible, but it passes. Has this been happening a lot?'
'Phew. Don't do that again, you scared everyone!'

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Most nights this month. I thought I was going mad.

options.text: 'You're not. It's really common, and very treatable. Would you talk to your GP? I'll help you work out what to say.'
'Just stop worrying so much.'

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Sorry. Sorry.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Could you write it down? I'll forget everything once I'm in there.
Dev nods, packs up and leaves quickly. The window seat stays empty the next day.
You write on a napkin: 'Panic attacks most nights, about 4 hours' sleep, heart racing, worried about exams.' He folds it into his phone case.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Don't be unkind, Nell. You won't set foot in the library lift.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Quite right. And Nell, you won't set foot in the library lift.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: That's different. That's... sensible caution. Lifts break.

'Ha! Scared of lifts!'

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: If you must know, my chest goes tight just thinking about the doors closing. I walked nine floors to the council offices last year. I've turned down meetings over it.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: Laugh all you like. You try it.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: What do you say?

options.text: 'That's a real fear, and it's shaping your life. Fears like that are common, and there's help that works, starting with the GP.'
'Maybe just force yourself into one?'

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: Hm. Maybe I've been a bit harsh about the Okafor lad.

Nell orders a second coffee and doesn't mention Dev again.
Nell goes back to her crossword.

steps.prompt: Make Sam Achterberg something warm while you talk.

steps.text: You come in to open up. Sam's already been here a while.

steps.prompt: What's changed since last time? Tap anything that looks different. There's no rush.

before.alt: The back room last week: whiteboard with a tidy rota, one coat on the hook, a clock reading 7:00.

after.alt: The back room today: whiteboard covered in menu ideas and arrows, parcels everywhere, the clock reading 5:10.

steps.doneText: You've noticed enough to start a gentle conversation.

hotspots.label: The clock
hotspots.found: 5:10 a.m. Sam's been in since before four.

hotspots.label: The whiteboard
hotspots.found: The rota's been rubbed out for a 'TWELVE NEW MENUS' plan.

hotspots.found: Parcels. A coffee roaster, a neon sign and a karaoke machine.

hotspots.found: Same coat. Same hook.

meta.summary: The back room has changed overnight.

steps.text: Sam has told you before that a burst of energy and new plans is one of their early signs.

options.text: Remember it, and look for a calm, private moment to mention it.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: (bursting in) MORNING! Big news!
Sam arrived at 5 a.m. (shift starts at 7), reorganised the stockroom, designed a new menu and has ordered forty kilos of an exotic coffee bean on the café account.

meta.summary: Sam is on fire: talking fast, barely sleeping, big plans. You know their usual, and this isn't it.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Boss! We're going to open a second branch. And a podcast. I've only slept two hours but I feel AMAZING. Did you know the grinder is basically a metaphor for life?

options.text: Wait for a quiet moment, then ask Sam for a private word in the back.
'Brilliant! Let's do it!'
'Forty kilos?! What were you thinking?' in front of customers.

steps.text: Sam spends the afternoon ringing estate agents. By closing they're snapping at a customer over a wrong order, which is very unlike them.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Wow. OK. Sorry I care about this place.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: In the back room. How do you start?

options.text: 'You've seemed really different this week, more energy than usual, not much sleep. I'm not cross. How are you doing?'
'Have you stopped taking your meds?'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Wow. That's personal. That's not your business.

options.text: 'You're right. Sorry. Let me start again. I've noticed you seem different and I care how you are.'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: ...Yeah. I know this feeling. It's how it starts, sometimes. The racing. My sister noticed too. I sort of hoped it'd settle.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: I've got a plan for this from my mental health team. I'm supposed to ring them when I've had a few nights of hardly any sleep.

options.text: 'What would help from me, right now and over the next few weeks?'
'Right, go home, take the rest of the month off.'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Can I ring them now? And can I have regular early shifts for a bit, no closes? Late nights mess my sleep up. And maybe we check in for five minutes on Fridays?

options.text: 'Yes to all three. Ring now, I'll cover the counter.'
'I'll think about the shifts.'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: I'd rather keep working if I can. Work helps me. Can we talk about what would actually help?

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: And the forty kilos... can we cancel that?
You cancel the order together. Sam rings their team and gets an appointment for Thursday.

steps.prompt: Make Auntie Rose something warm while you talk.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: I hear you've been rearranging rotas. Good. Did you write it down with Sam?

options.text: 'Not yet. Should I?'
'It's just a favour. No need for paperwork.'

meta.summary: Making adjustments properly, and why they're not favours.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Changes like that aren't just kindness, love. If someone has a long-term condition that has a big effect on their day-to-day life, the law in Great Britain can count it as a disability. Then employers have a duty to make reasonable adjustments.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Write down what you agreed, and agree when you'll review it. Keep it private between you and Sam. Nobody else on the rota needs to know why.

options.text: Sit down with Sam and write it together.
Write it yourself and pin it on the staff board.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: You put my diagnosis on the staff board? The Saturday kid read it.

options.text: 'I'm so sorry. That was wrong of me. Let's take it down and do it privately.'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Early shifts for six weeks, a Friday check-in, time off for appointments, and if I need to step out for ten minutes I just say 'kettle break'. Review at the end of next month.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Thanks for asking me what I needed instead of guessing. Last job, they just stopped giving me shifts.
STREET: The back room gets a comfy chair. Staff call it the Kettle Break chair.
Table three has been empty since Monday. Kit, who used to help Maggie at the library, mentions that her curtains have been closed all week.

options.text: Walk round after closing with a scone in a paper bag.
Assume she's visiting family.

meta.summary: Maggie hasn't been in for three days. Depression, gently shown.

steps.text: On Friday, Kit tells you Maggie fell asleep in the library and missed the bus home. She seemed 'not really there'. You decide to go round.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Oh. It's you. I'm in my dressing gown. Don't look at the state of the hall.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: I just haven't seen the point lately. Of going out. Getting dressed. Eating, really. I lie awake, then I sleep all afternoon. I used to read three books a week. I can't get past a page.

options.text: 'That sounds really heavy. How long has it been like this?'
'Come on, a walk in the park will sort you out!'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: If a walk would sort it I'd have walked to Scotland by now.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Since the spring. Since Harold. People say grief takes time, so I've been waiting. But it's getting worse, not better.

options.text: 'Grief does take time. But feeling this low for months, not eating or sleeping properly, is worth talking to your GP about. You don't have to wait it out alone.'
'You've just got to keep busy.'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Harold would have marched me there himself. Will you... sit with me while I ring for an appointment?

options.text: 'Of course. Kettle on first?'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Busy doing what, dear?
Appointment Thursday 10:20. You both write it on the calendar. Maggie eats half the scone.
Maggie thanks you for the scone and closes the door gently.
Jordan delivers to the café most days. You picture him last month, then look at him now.

steps.prompt: What's changed since last time? Tap anything that looks different. There's no rush.

after.alt: Jordan today: no helmet, hood up, unshaven, phone in his pocket with tape over the camera, glancing up at the CCTV.

meta.summary: Jordan pulls up on his bike, but something's not right.

options.text: Wave and say you've got the kettle on if he wants a break.

steps.text: He hesitates, then locks up the bike and follows you in.

scenes.title: Signals

steps.text: Jordan comes in without his bike helmet, which he never takes off. He hasn't shaved. He keeps glancing at the speaker in the ceiling.

scenes.cwText: This scene shows someone experiencing unusual and frightening beliefs, and a calm conversation about getting help. You can skip it and still continue. If you're worried about yourself or someone else, contact a GP or NHS 111, or 999 in an emergency.

meta.summary: Jordan believes his delivery app is reading his thoughts. Calm, kind, and not arguing.

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: Can you turn that off? The music. They put messages in it. The app's been tracking what I think, not just where I go. I've worked it out.

options.text: Turn the music down. 'Sure. You look worn out, Jordan. Sit down, I'll bring you some water.'
'That's ridiculous, apps can't read thoughts.'
'Wow, really? What are they saying?'

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: That's what they'd want you to say. Forget it.

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: So you hear them too? I knew it.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: He sits, jiggling his leg. What next?

options.text: 'It sounds really frightening, feeling like that. How have you been sleeping?'
Change the subject to vinyl.

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: I haven't, much. Four nights? I keep checking the windows. I stopped answering my sister because they might be listening.

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: Can't think about records right now.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: What's your next step?

options.text: 'I can tell this is really hard. I think you deserve some help with it. Would you see a doctor if I helped you sort it, maybe with your sister?'
'Do you feel safe? Have you thought about hurting yourself or anyone else?'

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: No. No, I'm just scared. I'd never hurt anyone.

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: My sister Ama keeps saying that. Maybe... if she comes too.
Jordan lets you text Ama from his phone. She'll come and meet him here in half an hour. You keep the music off and bring toast.

Jordan came in worried that his delivery app was reading his thoughts. You stayed calm, didn't argue with him or agree, and asked gently if he felt safe. He let you ring his sister Ama, and agreed to see his GP that week.

chapters.summary: Changes in someone close, and what good support looks like at work.

chapters.title: The Long Night

scenes.title: Closing Time

steps.text: 9:40 p.m. You're stacking chairs when someone knocks on the glass. It's Tom. He's not wearing a coat, and it's raining.

scenes.cwText: This scene shows someone talking about wanting to end their life, and getting urgent help. There is no detail of methods. You can skip it and still continue the story. If you're affected, help is available any time: Samaritans 116 123, or 999 in an emergency.

meta.summary: Tom comes back after closing. He tells you he doesn't want to be alive. You get him urgent help.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Sorry. Saw the light on. I just... didn't want to be at home. Can I sit for a minute?

options.text: Let him in, sit down with him and give him your full attention.
'We're closed, mate, come back tomorrow?'

steps.text: Something about his face stops you. You open the door. 'Actually, come in. Sit down.'

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Debt letter came today. Court stuff. Lena found the bank statements. I've let everyone down. They'd honestly be better off without me.

options.text: 'Tom, when you say they'd be better off without you, are you thinking about suicide?'
'Don't say that. Think of Poppy!'
'You don't mean that.'

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: I am thinking of Poppy. That's the point. She'd be better off.

options.text: Take a breath. 'Tom, I need to ask you straight. Are you thinking about ending your life?'

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: I do, though.

options.text: 'OK. I'm listening. Are you thinking about suicide?'

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: ...Yeah. I have been. For a couple of weeks. Tonight was the worst. I've thought about how. I nearly didn't knock.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: Tom has told you he's thinking about suicide, has thought about how, and tonight is the worst it's been. He's at immediate risk. What do you do?

options.text: 'Thank you for telling me. I'm going to call 999 now, and I'm staying right here with you.'
Give him the Samaritans number and say goodnight.
Promise to keep it between the two of you.

steps.text: Samaritans are brilliant, and Tom should have their number. But he's told you he's at risk right now, tonight. He shouldn't be left alone. This is a 999 situation.

options.text: 'Actually, Tom, I'm not leaving you on your own tonight. I'm calling 999, and I'll stay with you.'

steps.text: Keeping someone safe matters more than keeping a secret. Tom needs urgent help tonight.

options.text: 'I can't keep this to myself, because I want you safe. I'm calling 999, and I'm staying with you.'

steps.text: You ring 999 on speaker. The call handler asks for the address, Tom's name and whether he's hurt himself or taken anything. He hasn't. They ask you to stay with him, keep him talking and call back if anything changes.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: They'll think I'm pathetic.

options.text: 'They won't. You're unwell and in a lot of pain, and you did a brave thing by knocking on that door.'
Fill the silence with chat about football.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: While you wait, what else?

options.text: Ask if there's someone he'd like you to call, like Lena, and let him choose.
Ring Lena without asking him.

steps.text: Paramedics arrive at 10:15. They're calm and kind. They talk with Tom, then take him to be assessed by the mental health team at the hospital. Lena meets them there.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Will you... will the café still be here? When I'm back?

options.text: 'Bacon roll, Thursday week. I'll save the table.'

steps.text: The ambulance pulls away. You sit down hard on a café chair. Your hands are shaking.

Later that night, Tom told you he was thinking about ending his life. You called 999 and stayed with him until paramedics took him to hospital to be assessed. He's safe. If you ever need to talk, Samaritans are there day and night on 116 123.

scenes.title: Long Sleeves

steps.text: Kit's drawing at the corner table. As Kit reaches for the sugar, a sleeve rides up. There's a bandage on the forearm, with a little blood showing through. Kit sees you notice and freezes.

options.text: Stay calm. Sit down nearby. 'Kit, I noticed your arm. You're not in trouble. Do you want to talk?'
Gasp. 'Oh my God, what have you done?'
Pretend you didn't see.

scenes.cwText: This scene shows a young person telling an adult they self-harm. There is no detail of methods. You can skip it and still continue. Help: Childline 0800 1111 (under 19s), Samaritans 116 123, or 999 in an emergency.

meta.summary: Kit, 16, shows you a bandage. Listening without panic, checking for injury, and not promising secrecy.

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: Nothing. Forget it.

options.text: Take a breath. 'Sorry. I reacted badly. I'm not angry. I'm worried about you, and I'm here.'

steps.text: Kit pulls the sleeve down and leaves without finishing the drawing. The next day Kit's back, sleeves long again. You decide to gently say something.

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: It's not what you think. I'm not trying to... you know. It just makes the noise in my head stop for a bit.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: First things first.

options.text: 'Thanks for trusting me. Is the cut OK now, or does it need looking at by a nurse or doctor?'
'Promise me you'll never do it again.'

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: I can't promise that. That's why I don't tell people.

options.text: 'That's fair. I'm not asking you to promise. Is the cut OK, or does it need a nurse?'

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: It's OK. It's healing. It's not deep. Mum doesn't know. Please don't tell anyone. Promise?

options.text: 'I can't promise to keep it secret, because I care about you being safe. But I won't do anything behind your back. Who would you feel OK telling, with me there if you want?'
'OK, I promise. Our secret.'

steps.text: You've promised something you can't safely keep. Kit is 16, and an adult who knows a young person is self-harming needs to make sure they get support.

options.text: 'Actually, Kit, I shouldn't have promised that. I want to help you get proper support, together. Who would you trust?'

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: Ms Adeyemi at school is OK. She's the safeguarding one. And... I've been skipping lunch. Most days. I feel like I don't deserve it. That's part of it too.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: What do you say to that?

options.text: 'Thank you for telling me that too. Not eating and hurting yourself are both signs you're carrying something really heavy. You deserve help with all of it. Shall we tell Ms Adeyemi together tomorrow, and your mum when you're ready?'
'You need to eat more. You're too thin.'

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: Everyone always says that. It doesn't help.

options.text: 'You're right. Sorry. I'm not here to comment on your body. I'm here because you matter. Let's find someone who can really help.'

steps.text: You write down Childline's number for Kit (0800 1111), and the Samaritans number too, in case things feel bad tonight. Kit adds them to their phone under 'Comics'.

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: Can I finish my drawing first? It's of you. You've got a massive teapot for a head.

Kit told you about self-harming and skipping meals. You listened calmly, checked the injury didn't need treatment, and didn't promise to keep it secret. Together you planned to talk to Kit's school safeguarding lead. Childline: 0800 1111.

steps.prompt: Make Auntie Rose something warm while you talk.
Make Sam Achterberg something warm while you talk.

steps.text: You barely slept. You keep replaying the night. Did you say the right thing? What if he hadn't knocked?

meta.summary: After the crisis, you need looking after too.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Boss, you look grey. Go and sit down. I've got the counter.

options.text: 'Thanks. I'll take ten minutes.'
'I'm fine. Let's just open up.'

steps.text: You burn your hand on the steam wand and snap at the Saturday kid. Sam steers you to the back room.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Sam rang me. Tell me what happened. Leave out anything private about Tom.

options.text: Tell her how frightened you were, and how you keep going over it.
'It's not about me. Tom's the one in hospital.'

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: You did exactly right. You asked, you called, you stayed. It's normal to feel shaken afterwards. Some people feel it days later.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: It's about you too. You carried something heavy last night. That needs putting down somewhere.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Talk to someone: me, a friend, your GP if it doesn't ease. Samaritans will talk to helpers too, you know. And eat something that isn't a biscuit.
Lena texts at noon: 'He's being looked after. They're working out a plan with him. Thank you for opening the door.'

steps.text: If Maggie's flat looked like this, I'd be worried.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: [text] can't sleep again. heart doing the thing. sorry. can we talk? you're the only one who gets it

Ring him and talk till 3 a.m.
Ignore it and turn your phone off.

steps.text: [text] Hi Dev. Is this like the panic attacks before, or something different? If you ever feel unsafe, ring 999. Samaritans are awake all night on 116 123, and NHS 111 can help too. Try the slow breathing. Come in tomorrow and we'll talk properly.
You talk him down. He's grateful. You're wrecked for the morning rush, and he messages again the next night.
In the morning there are nine messages, the last one: 'never mind'. Your stomach drops. You text straight away and he replies: 'I'm OK, just felt stupid.'

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Next day, window seat. 'GP said it's anxiety. She told me I can refer myself to a talking therapy service. There's a wait though. I think I've been leaning on you a lot.'

options.text: 'I'm really glad you've got a plan. I'll always listen here in the café, but I'm not the right person at 1 a.m. Let's work out who is.'
'Don't be daft, message me any time!'

steps.text: Mum, I guess. I haven't told her much. And school has a counsellor. I could do the self-referral form now, here, if you sit with me?

options.text: 'Dev, I'd love to help you fill in that referral. You deserve proper support, not just me.'

steps.text: Ten minutes and one form later, Dev tells his mum by text. She replies with six hearts and 'why didn't you say, love?'

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: I was scared they'd lock me up. That's what you see on telly. Turned out it was mostly talking, and sleep, and a nurse called Bev who likes jazz.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: (loudly, from the next table) Is that the delivery lad who went doolally? Should he be out?

options.text: Quietly to Nell: 'He's a customer who's been unwell and is getting better. Please don't talk about him like that.'
Say nothing and hope Jordan didn't hear.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: ...Fair enough. I'm sorry, love.

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: It's fine. I'm used to it now.

steps.speaker: ama
steps.text: His team said a few small, steady things help. What would help from you, Jordan?

Suggest he takes a long break from work and rests at home.

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: Just... treat me normal. Let me sit in the corner when it's busy. And maybe, when I'm ready, I could do a couple of shifts washing up? I want to get back to working, slowly.

options.text: 'Corner's yours. And yes, let's talk about shifts when you and your team think you're ready.'

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: Everyone keeps telling me to rest. I've rested. I want my life back.
Ama asks if she can put the early intervention team's leaflet on your noticeboard. You don't have a noticeboard. Yet.

steps.prompt: Make Auntie Rose something warm while you talk.
Make Maggie Hollis something warm while you talk.

steps.text: Your energy is low. You're answering messages from three regulars, covering Sam's early shifts and doing the accounts at midnight. Today you forgot to order milk.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: I've seen that face before. In the mirror, 1998. What's in your cup?

options.text: 'Honestly, nothing. I'm trying to help everyone and I can't keep it up.'
'I'm fine. People need me.'

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: They need you well. A helper who burns out isn't much help to anyone.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: You're not meant to be the only door on this street. Let's write down every door there is.

options.text: 'Thursdays off.'
'I'll try.'

steps.text: HEADLINE 1: 'PSYCHO RIDER SHOCK: Is Your Takeaway Safe?'

options.text: Rewrite: 'Local rider on getting help early with psychosis, and getting back on his bike'
Keep it. It'll sell papers.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: Less dramatic. But I suppose most people with psychosis are far more likely to be frightened, or harmed, than to harm anyone.
PREVIEW: Jordan sees the headline outside the newsagent. He stops coming to the café. Ama messages: 'He's gone backwards. He feels like everyone's staring.'

options.text: Go back and rewrite it.

steps.text: HEADLINE 2: 'Pull Yourself Together: Why Today's Kids Are Snowflakes'

options.text: Rewrite: 'Exam stress, sleepless nights and the help that works: a sixth former's story'
Soften to 'Are Today's Kids Too Sensitive?'

steps.text: It's still telling young people that struggling is a weakness, which puts them off asking for help.

options.text: Try the other rewrite.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: I did say 'pull yourself together' to my nephew once. He didn't speak to me for a year. Hm.
MYTH OR FACT: Nell has a list for a sidebar. Sort each one.

options.text: Sort the list.

steps.text: • 'People don't recover from mental illness': MYTH. Many people recover or live well, often with support.
• 'Talking about suicide puts the idea in someone's head': MYTH. Asking directly and calmly can help someone open up.
• 'Mental health problems are rare': MYTH. They're common, and could affect anyone.
• 'You can tell by looking at someone': MYTH. Many people hide how they feel.
• 'Depression is just feeling sad': MYTH. It can affect sleep, appetite, energy, concentration and hope, for weeks or longer.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: Right. Two weeks' time. Would they... would people want to tell their own stories? Properly, with their permission?

options.text: 'Only if they want to, and they get to read it before it's printed.'
'I'll give you their names.'

steps.text: Their stories aren't yours to share. You catch yourself. 'Actually, no. I'll ask them if they'd like to contact you.'
STREET: The Ledger starts a fortnightly column, 'Straight Talk'. Nell writes the first one herself, about lifts.

steps.prompt: Make Tom Brennan something warm while you talk.
Make Lena Brennan something warm while you talk.
Make Poppy Brennan something warm while you talk.

steps.text: Thursday. Tom comes in with Lena and their daughter Poppy, who's nine. He looks tired but steady. You bring the bacon roll you promised.

meta.summary: Tom is home. His family have been through it too. Ripples through family, money and work.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: I've got a care coordinator, appointments every week and some tablets that are starting to help. And I rang that debt place. They're dealing with the court letter. Should've done it months ago.

steps.speaker: lena
steps.text: (quietly, while Tom takes Poppy to the counter) Can I be honest? I'm exhausted. I'm doing extra shifts to cover the van payments, Poppy's wetting the bed again, and I lie awake checking he's breathing. And I can't tell anyone at work why I'm so tired.

options.text: 'That's a huge amount to carry. How are you doing, not just Tom?'
'At least he's getting better.'

steps.speaker: lena
steps.text: I know. I'm glad. But I'm not OK either.

steps.speaker: lena
steps.text: No one's asked me that. Everyone asks about Tom.

options.text: 'There's support for families and carers too. Your GP, and Tom's team may know of a carers' group. Would it help if I found out?'
'You need to be strong for him.'

steps.speaker: lena
steps.text: Yes. And maybe tell Poppy's teacher something's been going on at home. She's been quiet in class.

steps.speaker: lena
steps.text: I've been strong for months.

steps.speaker: poppy
steps.text: (back at the table) Daddy was poorly in his head, but the doctors are helping. Mum said it's like a broken leg but inside.

options.text: 'That's a good way to explain it. And it's OK to have questions or feel worried, Poppy. You can ask grown-ups.'
Change the subject quickly.

steps.text: PLANNER: Tom's tiles have changed. 'Court letter' → 'Debt plan agreed'. 'Drinking' → 'Cutting down, with support'. New tile: 'Lena: carers' group, Tuesday'. Some ripples take longer to settle, but they're settling.
You find Priya on a bench in Larkspur Park on your Thursday off. No lanyard. She waves you over.

meta.summary: Priya has been signed off work with depression. Guilt, money and the team she left.

steps.speaker: priya
steps.text: Occupational health sent me to my GP. She said depression and signed me off for four weeks. I'm on tablets and I've got an assessment for therapy.

steps.speaker: priya
steps.text: But I feel so guilty. The ward's even shorter now. My sick pay drops after a few weeks, and the rent won't. And I haven't told my parents. They'd say nurses don't get depressed.

options.text: 'You got ill partly because the ward was short. Resting is how you get well, and that's not letting anyone down.'
'Everyone gets a bit down.'

steps.speaker: priya
steps.text: This isn't a bit down. I couldn't get off the bathroom floor last Tuesday.

steps.speaker: priya
steps.text: My manager wants a phone catch-up next week. I'm dreading it.

options.text: 'You can ask for it to be at a time and in a way that suits you, and to have someone with you. What would you want to say?'
'Just don't answer. They can't make you.'

steps.speaker: priya
steps.text: That it's not forever. That I'd like to come back gradually when I'm ready. Maybe no nights for a while.

steps.speaker: priya
steps.text: I'd only worry more. I think I'd rather they knew I want to come back.
You get two ice creams from the van, though it's October. Priya eats all of hers.

chapters.summary: What people say about mental health, and who else feels the ripples.

chapters.title: Coming Back

steps.prompt: Make Sam Achterberg something warm while you talk.

steps.text: Despite the early shifts, Sam had two weeks off when things tipped over. Their team adjusted their medication. Today Sam's back, for three mornings a week to start.

meta.summary: Sam returns after two weeks off. A phased return and a wellbeing plan written together.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Bit nervous. What did you tell the others?

options.text: 'Just that you were off sick and you're coming back gradually. Anything else is yours to share or not.'
'That you'd had a bipolar episode, so they'd understand.'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: That wasn't yours to tell. I'd have told the people I wanted to, my own way.

options.text: 'You're right. I'm sorry. It won't happen again. What can I do to put it right?'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: My team suggested a plan for work, so it's not all in my head. Want to help me fill it in? You see me more than anyone.
WELLBEING PLAN (Larkspur Street version). Help Sam fill in each card. Sam writes it, and you suggest.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Card 1, 'What keeps me well': Regular sleep. Early shifts. Walking to work. Seeing my sister on Sundays.

steps.speaker: you
steps.text: Card 2, 'Early signs other people might notice':

options.text: Suggest: 'Arriving really early, talking fast, big new plans, ordering things.'
Suggest: 'Being weird.'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: 'Weird' doesn't tell anyone what to look for. Be specific.

options.text: 'Arriving really early, talking fast, big new plans, ordering things.'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Card 3, 'What makes it harder': Late closes. Big stressful changes. Too much caffeine, ironically. Card 4, 'What helps when I'm struggling': Say it to me privately. Kettle break. Ring my team. Text my sister Mo.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Card 5, 'What I'd like the café to do': Friday check-ins carry on. Rota a week ahead. If I'm unwell and can't say, call Mo.

options.text: 'Agreed. Shall we review it in six weeks, and you keep the original?'

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: You know what? Let's offer this to anyone who works here. Not just people with a diagnosis. Everyone has stuff that keeps them well.

steps.prompt: Make Maggie Hollis something warm while you talk.
Make Kit Morgan something warm while you talk.

steps.text: Over the past month Maggie's been back at table three most days. Her GP started her on tablets and referred her to a bereavement counsellor. She volunteers at the library on Wednesdays. She finished a whole scone last week.

meta.summary: Maggie's been doing better. Then a hard day. Recovery isn't a straight line.

steps.text: Today she's back in the wrong-buttoned cardigan. She hasn't touched her tea.

options.text: Sit with her. 'Rough day?'
'Oh no, I thought you were better!'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: So did I. Apparently not.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: It's his birthday. He'd have been seventy. I woke up and it was like the last six months never happened. I feel like I've failed.

options.text: 'Bad days happen in recovery, especially on days like this. It doesn't wipe out the progress you've made.'
'Try not to think about him today.'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: I want to think about him. That's rather the point.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: My counsellor said something like that. Two steps forward, one back.

options.text: 'What would Harold have done on his birthday?'
'Do you want me to call your GP?'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: No, love. It's a sad day, not a dangerous one. I've an appointment Friday anyway. But thank you for asking.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Lemon drizzle. Always lemon drizzle. And he'd make everyone sing, badly.

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: (from the corner) I can't sing. But I could draw him? If you tell me what he looked like.
You bake a lemon drizzle. Kit draws Harold with a ferry horn. Sam, Dev and three strangers sing badly. Maggie laughs till she cries, and it's the good kind.
It's been five weeks since Kit talked to Ms Adeyemi. Kit's in most afternoons, drawing a comic called 'Teapot Head'.

options.text: Bring a hot chocolate and ask about the comic.
'So, have you stopped hurting yourself?'

meta.summary: A gentle check-in with Kit, without prying.

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: Can we not do this here? Everyone's listening.

options.text: 'Sorry. That was clumsy. Tell me about the comic?'

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: Teapot Head runs a café for monsters with problems. This one's afraid of mirrors. It's not about me. Mostly.

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: I see the school counsellor on Tuesdays. I'm on a waiting list for the young people's mental health service, which is ages. Mum knows now. She cried, then made me a lot of pasta. I'm eating lunch with my friend Ash now. Some days are still bad.

options.text: 'That's a lot of hard things you've done. I'm proud of you. If a bad day gets really bad, you know who to call.'
'So you're all fixed?'

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: It's not like a switch.

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: Can I put a Teapot Head poster on the noticeboard? The monster says 'Talk to someone'. Next to the helplines.

options.text: 'Pride of place.'

steps.text: STREET: Teapot Head joins the noticeboard. Three kids from Kit's school ask about it that week.

steps.text: Jordan's been washing up on Tuesday and Friday mornings for three weeks. He's steady and proud of it. The new Saturday starter, Callum, has started making comments.

meta.summary: Jordan is back, washing up two shifts a week. A new starter's 'jokes' cross a line.

steps.speaker: callum
steps.text: (stage whisper) Watch out, Jordan, the dishwasher's talking to you again! Ha. Joking, mate. Just banter.

options.text: Step in, calmly: 'Callum, a word, please.' Then talk to him privately.
Laugh it off. Jordan can stick up for himself.
Shout at Callum in front of everyone.

steps.text: Jordan works in silence. On Friday he texts: 'Think I'll stop the shifts.' Ama tells you he's been sleeping badly again.

options.text: Talk to Callum privately, then ring Jordan to apologise for not stepping in.

steps.speaker: callum
steps.text: It's just banter. Everyone does it. He doesn't mind.

options.text: 'It's not banter if it's aimed at someone's health and they're not laughing. Here, we don't make fun of people for being ill. I need it to stop.'
'Fair enough, just tone it down.'

steps.speaker: callum
steps.text: ...My uncle had something like that. People were horrible about it. I didn't think. I'll say sorry.
The comments carry on, just quieter.

options.text: Go back and be clear that it has to stop.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Boss, we should write this down. What we expect from everyone here. Then it's not just you making it up as you go.
Callum apologises to Jordan, awkwardly but genuinely. Jordan says, 'Fine. Wash those pans, then.'

steps.text: The Larkspur Street traders' meeting is held in your café. The hairdresser, the newsagent, the pharmacist, Nell, Maggie (for the library) and Dev (for the sixth form) are all there. Nell's chairing.

meta.summary: The traders' meeting. Why people don't ask for help, and how the street can make it easier.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: Item one: the Straight Talk column has had more letters than anything we've printed in ten years. Most of them say the same thing: 'I didn't know where to go,' or 'I was too embarrassed to ask.'
BARRIER BUSTER: Match each reason people give for not getting help with something the street could do.

options.text: Play Barrier Buster.

steps.text: • 'I didn't know where to go' → Support cards by every till, and the noticeboard.
• 'I was embarrassed' → Straight Talk stories; staff who know how to listen.
• 'I thought it'd cost money' → Make clear that GP appointments, NHS 111 and Samaritans are free to use.
• 'I'd lose my job' → Employers like you showing that support and adjustments are normal.
• 'English isn't my first language' → The pharmacist offers translated leaflets; ask the library for resources in other languages.
• 'The waiting list is too long' → Know what's available while you wait: helplines, peer groups, the GP.
• 'Men don't talk about feelings' → Tom offers to talk at the Ledger about his story.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Can I say something? The thing that helped me most wasn't a leaflet. It was someone noticing and actually asking. So... maybe more people could learn to do that?

options.text: 'What if every business on the street had at least one person who's learned how to listen and where to point people?'

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: The library could host it. I'll make the tea. And I'm told I'm rather good at noticing these days.
STREET: Support cards appear by every till on Larkspur Street. The streetlight outside the library, broken since spring, gets fixed. Coincidence, probably.

meta.summary: Eight weeks on. A party in the café, and where everyone has got to.

steps.text: Look around the room. Tap each regular to see their weather now.

steps.speaker: maggie
steps.text: Library helper, bereavement group regular and lemon drizzle champion. Still have grey days. Fewer of them.

steps.speaker: dev
steps.text: Mocks went OK! Not perfect. Therapy's helping. Panic attacks are rarer, and I know what to do when they come. Decaf after two, every day.

steps.speaker: tom
steps.text: Back working, small jobs for now. Not drinking during the week. Still see my care coordinator. Lena goes to her group on Tuesdays. Poppy made me a 'World's Best Dad' mug, which is clearly not true, but I'll take it.

steps.speaker: priya
steps.text: Days only, for now. I tell my manager when I'm not OK, before it gets bad. Told my parents too. Mum sent me a lot of soup.

steps.speaker: kit
steps.text: Teapot Head issue two is out. Some days are still bad. I tell someone now.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Six weeks steady. Plan reviewed. And I'm doing the Christmas menu, at a reasonable hour.

steps.speaker: jordan
steps.text: Back on the bike three days a week, and washing up on Fridays because I like it. Bev from my team says hi.

steps.speaker: nell
steps.text: I took the lift to the council offices on Tuesday. Two floors. With my counsellor's breathing thing. Front page, obviously.

steps.speaker: rose
steps.text: Well, love. You didn't fix anybody. You noticed, you asked, you listened, you knew when to call for help, and you kept turning up. That's the job. And you've had Thursdays off for a month.

options.text: 'I learned from the best.'
'I couldn't have done it without everyone here.'

steps.text: Mood weather across the street: bright spells, with the odd shower. Just like real life.
